blocks.heading: Pricing strategies fit circumstances
blocks.text: Cost-plus pricing adds a mark-up to a relevant unit-cost base. Penetration sets a low initial price to encourage market entry and customer trial. Skimming sets a high initial price for a distinctive new offering where some buyers will pay, often reducing it later. Competitive pricing uses rivals’ prices as a reference. Promotional pricing makes a temporary price reduction or special offer. Choose according to objectives, demand, competition, costs, product and capacity. A strategy is a pricing approach, not proof of customer response. A low price cannot compensate for an unwanted or unavailable product.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Fictional Teya Drink enters a competitive local market with a familiar product, while fictional Omi Devices introduces a distinctive design valued by a small early market. Penetration may help Teya attract trial if it can afford the low price; skimming may suit Omi only if the distinctive benefit supports willingness to pay and rivals cannot immediately remove it.

blocks.heading: Cost-plus pricing
blocks.text: Cost-plus pricing adds a specified mark-up to an appropriate unit-cost base. It offers a clear starting rule and can cover the included cost if the resulting price is actually paid, but ignores demand and rival prices if used alone. A wrong or incomplete cost base can mislead. Mark-up is on cost; margin is on sales revenue.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Fictional Ota Cups adds a 20% mark-up to full unit cost. The rule is straightforward, but the business must check whether buyers accept the resulting price and whether costs remain accurate.

blocks.heading: Penetration pricing
blocks.text: Penetration pricing uses a low initial price to encourage entry, trial and market share. It may suit a familiar product with strong competition and price-sensitive buyers if the firm can finance the low return and supply the extra demand. It risks weak margins, a low-price image and customers resisting later rises. Extra volume is not guaranteed and more sales do not automatically mean more profit.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Fictional Teya Juice enters a competitive local market and can supply a limited trial at a low introductory price. The low entry price may encourage switching, but the owner should monitor margins and capacity and explain any later normal price clearly.

blocks.heading: Price skimming
blocks.text: Price skimming uses a high initial price for a new distinctive offering where early buyers are willing to pay, often lowering it later as the market develops. It may help recover development spending and capture a high return per early unit. It requires credible differentiation and can attract competitors or restrict demand. A high price without a valued distinctive benefit is not enough.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Fictional Hena Devices has a new design valued by a small group of early buyers and few close substitutes initially. Skimming may suit that early demand, but the firm should reassess as rivals appear rather than assume the high price can continue indefinitely.

blocks.heading: Competitive pricing
blocks.text: Competitive pricing uses rival prices as a reference when setting the firm’s price. It can help where customers compare similar offerings, but the firm’s costs, quality and service may differ. Matching a rival below a sustainable cost can harm the business. It does not mean every firm must charge exactly the same amount or ignore differentiation.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Fictional Oru Stationery compares prices for a standard notebook sold by several local shops. A similar price can avoid an unexplained premium, while availability or service may justify some difference. Check Oru’s own cost before matching a rival.

blocks.heading: Promotional pricing
blocks.text: Promotional pricing offers a temporary reduced or special price to stimulate a response, such as trial or clearing suitable stock. It differs from a continuing low entry strategy in its temporary promotional purpose. It reduces revenue per unit and may bring purchases forward rather than create lasting demand. Clear duration and conditions matter, and repeated offers can train customers to wait for discounts.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Fictional Nela Cases offers one week’s discount on its established range. The temporary offer may encourage purchases now, but management should compare added contribution and promotion cost rather than equate more units with higher profit.

blocks.heading: Worked practice: Marketing choices in a coherent mix
blocks.text:
Fictional Tula Tea has full unit cost N$80 and uses a 50% mark-up on cost for its normal price. It considers a temporary 25% reduction from that price. Local buyers know where to buy but are unsure about the new flavour. Controlled sampling at its collection point is affordable; a broad campaign costs much more. No increase in paid demand is yet confirmed.

a Explain how Tula’s pricing and promotion choices interact with its stated customer barrier and costs. [8]
b Evaluate a temporary price cut against controlled sampling as the next step. [12]

a Cost-plus gives N$120 normal price; the 25% reduction gives N$90 and reduces the amount above stated unit cost from N$40 to N$10. More units would therefore be needed to preserve a given surplus before new campaign costs, and no volume increase is confirmed. Sampling addresses taste uncertainty directly; a price cut may not resolve that uncertainty. Promotion should fit the actual barrier and preserve feasible supply. b A lower price could encourage trial but reduces the return on each sold unit and may attract temporary bargain demand. Controlled sampling lets buyers experience the flavour without reducing the price on every qualifying sale, although samples and administration cost money. Given known location and uncertain taste, start with an affordable limited sample trial, measure paid conversion and reassess price evidence. Do not claim higher profit merely from a lower price or count samples as sales. If affordability proves decisive, test a sustainable price response instead.

blocks.heading: Worked practice: Marketing choices in a coherent mix
blocks.text:
Fictional Tula Tea has full unit cost N$80 and uses a 50% mark-up on cost for its normal price. It considers a temporary 25% reduction from that price. Local buyers know where to buy but are unsure about the new flavour. Controlled sampling at its collection point is affordable; a broad campaign costs much more. No increase in paid demand is yet confirmed.

a(i) Define cost-plus pricing. [2]
a(ii) State two factors affecting promotion choice. [2]
b State two initial pricing strategies for a new product. [2]
c Calculate Tula’s normal and proposed promotional prices. [6]
d Evaluate sampling against the broad campaign for the stated barrier. [8]

a(i) Adding a specified mark-up to a relevant unit-cost base. a(ii) Target access and available budget. b Penetration and skimming. c Mark-up = 80 × 0.50 = N$40. Normal price = 80 + 40 = N$120. Discount = 120 × 0.25 = N$30. Promotional price = 120 − 30 = N$90. The customer saving is N$30 and the price remains N$10 above the stated unit cost before any new campaign cost. d Sampling directly addresses uncertain taste among relevant local buyers, while the broad campaign mainly adds awareness they already have. Samples cost money and do not prove paid demand, but a controlled trial limits that exposure. Prefer sampling with clear price and purchase information, then review conversion; choose wider advertising if evidence later shows lack of awareness is the actual barrier.

blocks.heading: Worked practice: Marketing choices in a coherent mix
blocks.text:
Fictional Omi Snacks sells at N$50 with stated full unit cost N$35. Buyers know the outlet but are uncertain about taste. It compares affordable controlled sampling with a broad awareness campaign and a temporary 10% price reduction.

Evaluate Omi’s sampling, awareness campaign and price offer under the original facts. Give a concise plan. [12]

Barrier: taste uncertainty, while location awareness already exists. Price calculation: 10% of N$50 is N$5, so the offer price is N$45, leaving N$10 above stated N$35 cost before new promotion cost instead of N$15 normally. Sampling directly tests taste but has cost and uncertain conversion. Broad awareness spending may miss the real obstacle. Judgement: controlled sampling first, with honest purchase information and paid-response review; change priority if evidence identifies price as the problem.
